doc.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997

title: Changes in audiences and the club scene
summary: Why clubs declined: urban safety, concert halls and big fees.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: It’s interesting to think I guess in the ‘40s and when this kind of music was the popular music, that with all the bands touring and so forth, that it certainly has changed.

Well there’s still a big audience for this kind of music but everybody’s a little afraid to come out anymore. You know like they think the cops are going to be there busting them if they have a drink and that kind of thing. And they stay home, they play their records.

Life has changed drastically. I mean it used to be where the urban situation was centrally located. It was easy. There were a lot of people there, there was a certain amount of security, you didn’t have to worry about being bowled over by a bunch of thugs or by some gang members. I mean there was still problems but in any large city that’s going to happen. But there seemed to be a certain amount of safety or you felt secure going downtown. A lot of bright lights, everything was there. The theaters, the restaurants, the jazz clubs, the little bars. You seemed to know everybody. They’ve done away with that. If you want to go somewhere to hear music you have to drive clear across town to some dark little shopping plaza that’s closed except for this one thing, and park like a quarter of a mile away—
Or else you go to a concert hall. I think some of the things that ruined the whole club scene were the concert halls and the big money that these bands demanded.
Thousands and thousands of dollars you know.
Not to mention what they’re presenting as jazz in the concert halls.
